articles.title: Sandpapergate: Cummins, Bancroft, Lehmann, Warner - who said what about Australia scandal?
articles.summary: As Cameron Bancroft's explosive allegations raise more questions about the sandpaper scandal, BBC Sport looks at who was there and what they have said since.
articles.body:
The sandpaper scandal, one of the biggest controversies in the history of Test cricket, continues to engulf Australian sport.

Fresh evidence from Cameron Bancroft - the culprit of the ball-tampering in South Africa in 2018 - has heaped pressure on Australia captain Pat Cummins, former coach Darren Lehmann and Cricket Australia.

In a detailed account of more than 4,000 words published in the West Australian newspaper, Bancroft alleges all the Australia players and coaches present in Cape Town eight years ago knew of the plot.

Bancroft's explosive testimony supports claims made by Usman Khawaja, David Warner and Chadd Sayers.

However, Cummins denied Khawaja's version of events in his own extraordinary news conference in Sydney last week. Cummins spoke to the media for 68 minutes in an address broadcast on live television.

Here, BBC Sport collects the most recent accounts of players and coaches involved in the saga that became widely known as sandpapergate.

Batter Khawaja played all four Tests in South Africa and a total of 88 for Australia before retiring from international cricket earlier this year.

Revelations in his autobiography reignited debate around the sandpaper scandal and made headlines across the globe.

"It was all of us," Khawaja said. "Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us.

"In an ideal world, I don't want to do this. I don't want to be the one who comes out and talks about the truth. The issue is that I genuinely thought after eight years the truth would have been out by now.

"Even in the change rooms when I was talking to them after the game. I said, 'Take this as a team'.

"We did this as a team. We knew what was going on, and we have to take it as a team, and so I was always of that stance."

Whole Australia team knew of sandpaper use - Khawaja

Warner was Australia's opening batter and vice-captain during the 2018 series. He, along with captain Steve Smith and Bancroft, were the three players punished for the ball-tampering.

The Cricket Australia (CA) investigation in 2018 found Warner developed the plan and that he instructed Bancroft to carry out the cheating.

After serving his ban, Warner returned to play a further 133 times for Australia across formats, including three Ashes series and the 2023 World Cup win. He retired from international cricket in 2024.

In response to Khawaja's book, Warner said: "I thank you for what you've done. It's 100% accurate what you've said. Now everyone knows the truth."

He also accused Cricket Australia of a cover-up, describing the CA investigation as "rushed" and botched".

"As far as l am aware, CA did not interview Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc or Nathan Lyon in their 2018 investigation," Warner said.

"If that's correct, then how can CA push the idea that the bowlers didn't know?"

Warner accuses Cricket Australia of 'cover-up'

The Cape Town Test was the 13th of Cummins' Test career. A key bowler, he would go on to be named Australia's Test captain in 2021. It is a position he still holds.

Prior to Khawaja's book, Cummins and the other bowlers from Cape Town - Hazlewood, Starc and Lyon - had always denied knowledge of the plan to use sandpaper.

In an extraordinary news conference last week, Cummins called Khawaja's claims that the whole team knew about the plan "100% wrong" and "utter nonsense".

"I said that consistently for the last eight years," Cummins said. "I did not know that was happening.

"He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball-tamper with sandpaper. That's complete and utter nonsense."

Asked if he knew of any plans at any stage to tamper with the ball during the series against South Africa, Cummins said: "No."

Cummins also said he did not remember a meeting where Khawaja had called on the team to take collective responsibility - something his former team-mate claimed.

Opening batter Bancroft was playing his eighth Test in Cape Town, aged 25. He was the player caught using sandpaper on the field.

He played another two Tests after serving his ban and is still playing for Western Australia. He turns 34 this week.

In 2021, Bancroft said it was "self-explanatory" whether the bowlers knew of the plan, and on Wednesday he backed Khawaja's account, saying Cummins' news conference made him "feel angry, betrayed and alone".

Like Khawaja, Bancroft said sandpaper was first used during the second Test against South Africa – the match before he was caught - and also said he had conversations with the Australia seamers about whether the ball was "swinging enough".

He said the entire playing group and staff had "celebrations" about the effect of the sandpaper. He also claimed that coach Lehmann and bowling coach David Saker were present in the initial discussions and that Bancroft's role was also discussed in a team meeting before day three.

In an account published by the West Australian on Wednesday, Bancroft wrote: "All the bowlers gave me feedback if my work on the ball was working. It was helpful.

"Is it going yet? It's not going yet, it needs more. So I would use the sandpaper more on the ball.

"There was even a time I was told to stop out of fear what I was doing was becoming too obvious."

Bancroft sandpaper claims heap pressure on Cummins

Lehmann was Australia coach at the time of the scandal. He was cleared by the CA investigation and said he had "no prior knowledge" of the plan to ball-tamper.

He resigned after the series and has been Northamptonshire coach since the start of the 2025 English season.

After Khawaja's revelations, Lehmann said: "I don't think everyone would have known [about the use of sandpaper]. You do know ball-tampering is going on because it's been happening for 150 years."

After Cricket Australia said it would hold an open forum, Lehmann said he has "nothing to hide".

Speaking on radio coverage of the third one-day international against England after Bancroft's account was published, Lehmann said: "I need to sit back, process it and work through each allegation.

"That's what I'll be doing over the next few days.

"I need to have a really good read of it. I need to make sure I'm saying what I want to say."

Smith, one of the greatest batters of his generation, was Australia's captain at the time of the scandal.

After serving a 12-month ban, he returned for the World Cup and Ashes the following year and has stood in as captain at times since.

He was found to have been aware of the plan to cheat and to mislead the public and match officials.

Smith, who broke down in tears when apologising at a subsequent news conference, as cameras captured the emotional toll of the moment, has not spoken publicly since Khawaja's book was published.

Speaking about the episode in September this year, he said: "That was a traumatic experience in my life and when I hear the flash of a camera it makes me revisit that in a way.

"I've tried to kind of erase a lot of 2018 and what happened. I can't remember a lot about the series. I've tried to block most of it out of my memory bank."

Marsh was bowling when Bancroft was caught using sandpaper on the ball in Cape Town. As an all-rounder, he was not part of the 2021 bowlers' statement.

Marsh was captain during Australia's recent ODI series against England and refused to answer questions on the topic before the series opener.

"I am not here to share mine [story] today," he said.

"I respect Uzzie [Khawaja] has told his story; my focus is on tomorrow. I am not here to go back on South Africa."

Following the conclusion of the series, Marsh did not take part in his post-match news conference, with 26-year-old bowler Jack Edwards taking his place.

Paine was Australia's wicketkeeper during the South Africa series and was made captain when Smith was banned.

He served in the role until he stood down in 2021 over a historical investigation into sexually explicit text messages sent to a female colleague.

In his autobiography, Paine said the suggestion everyone in the Australia dressing room must have known about the sandpaper use is "rubbish" and claimed he first found out when images appeared on the big screen in Cape Town.

"Everyone out there was shocked when they looked up on the big screen and saw Cameron Bancroft with a piece of sandpaper in his hand," Paine wrote. "I was stunned. We all were.

"My heart sank, I was thinking, 'What the f***?' A sense of dread came over us all."

Bancroft said he discussed whether the ball was reversing with Paine during the second Test.

Saker was Australia's bowling coach during the South Africa series.

Bancroft alleged Saker was present for discussions about the use of sandpaper and told the batter he needed to do more to the ball.

Saker was also England bowling coach as recently as last month's tri-series in Pakistan. He was an influential part of England's 2010-11 Ashes win.

In 2021, reflecting on the sandpaper saga, Saker said: "Obviously a lot of things went wrong at that time. There was a lot of people to blame. It could have been me to blame, it could have been someone else. It could have been stopped and it wasn't, which is unfortunate.

"Cameron's a very nice guy. He's just doing it to get something off his chest… He's not going to be the last. You could point your finger at me, you could point your finger at Boof [Lehmann]. Could you point it at other people? Of course you could.

"The disappointing thing is it's never going to go away. Regardless of what's said. We all know that we made a monumental mistake. The gravity wasn't as plain until it all came out."

Starc was an integral part of the vaunted Australia attack in Cape Town and remains so in the present day. He is ranked as the number one bowler in Test cricket by the International Cricket Council.

Left-armer Starc repeatedly denied knowledge of the sandpaper plot, including in the statement released with Cummins, Hazlewood and Lyon in 2021, and in a news conference in the days after Khawaja's claims emerged.

Speaking on 10 November, Starc said: "Obviously, there's differing opinions of eight years ago. We were heavily grilled through the process at the time, and since, and I guess I won't speak on behalf of the bowlers, but where I stand, my opinion hasn't changed. My recollection hasn't changed from what we said in 2021.

"I'll stick to what I said five years ago, what I said at the time, eight years ago. Clearly, there's different versions from different people, and I'll leave it where I left it back then."

Along with Cummins and Starc, Hazlewood and Lyon have remained part of Australia's first-choice bowling unit in the eight years since the sandpaper scandal, forming one of the greatest four-man attacks in Test history.

Seamer Hazlewood and off-spinner Lyon joined Cummins and Starc in releasing a statement in 2021, responding to an interview given by Bancroft to the Guardian newspaper when he said the bowlers' involvement in the sandpaper plot was "self-explanatory".

Neither Hazlewood nor Lyon has spoken publicly since the fresh claims from Khawaja, Warner and Bancroft emerged.

Their statement released with Cummins and Starc in 2021 said: "We pride ourselves on our honesty. So it's been disappointing to see that our integrity has been questioned by some journalists and past players in recent days in regard to the Cape Town Test of 2018.

"We did not know a foreign substance was taken onto the field to alter the condition of the ball until we saw the images on the big screen at Newlands.

"We respectfully request an end to the rumour-mongering and innuendo. It has gone on too long and it is time to move on."

A swing bowler, Sayers played his only Test for Australia after the sandpaper controversy erupted – the fourth and final match of the series against South Africa in Johannesburg.

Sayers, who retired from first-class cricket in 2021, spoke to Australian radio station SEN in the aftermath of Khawaja's claims, to corroborate the former batter's account.

Sayers claimed to have removed sandpaper from the field in the second Test against South Africa, the match before Bancroft was caught. He also backed up Khawaja's assertion that the entire Australia squad discussed the sandpaper issue after it was revealed in Cape Town.

Speaking on 15 November, Sayers said: "I am comfortable sitting here that I believe everyone in that side knew what was going on and what was being used.

"It was used in two Test matches and there were discussions in the changing rooms.

"After the occurrence in Cape Town, we all sat in the changing rooms after that day's play and, probably for 60 to 90 minutes, we talked about what had happened and I guess where to next."

Spinner Holland, who retired in 2021, was also a back-up bowler on the trip.

He also said there was a meeting held in the fallout from Cape Town about players taking responsibility.

"Once we got back to the hotel we did sit as a group [to discuss] what had happened and who was going to take the blame," Holland told newspaper The Australian.

"To Davey's [Warner's] credit, from what I remember, he did put his hand up and say he would take some of the responsibility, but not all of it.

"To be sitting there and seeing three blokes hung out to dry when you are supposed to be part of a team was a pretty hard watch."

Australia's Sayers 'took sandpaper from field'

Batter Handscomb was Australia's 12th man on the day Bancroft was caught, making frequent trips between the field and the dressing room.

Bancroft's account alleges Handscomb was told by Lehmann, via walkie-talkie, to "get the sandpaper off Bangers [Bancroft] now".

Last week, following Khawaja's claims but before Bancroft spoke, Handscomb was asked for his recollections after making a century for Victoria in the Sheffield Shield against Western Australia.

On 11 November, Handscomb said: "I appreciate you have to ask these questions. I've had a nice day today, it's not really something that I want to comment on right now. I'll sort of just let the powers of be do their thing."

Former England batter Hick was part of the Australia backroom team on the South Africa tour of 2018.

Hick was made redundant by Cricket Australia as part of a series of cost-cutting measures in 2020.

Speaking to the Sydney Morning Herald last week, Hick said: "I have seen the various statements around the coaches, and I'm very disappointed with the broad nature of them.

"Khawaja puts it simply: 'It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us'. To me, what Khawaja is implying here is absolutely false.

"In regard to any discussions around the ball-tampering in Port Elizabeth or Cape Town, I will say in true honesty that I did not hear or know anything.

"My first knowledge of all this was, like many, when it appeared on the big screen in Cape Town as I was sat on the outside balcony at the time."

Australian cricket was rocked by the sandpapergate scandal in 2018 and it is back in the headlines in 2026 following fresh allegations by former Australia batter Usman Khawaja.

articles.title: Sandpapergate: Australia Test captain Pat Cummins faces fresh scrutiny after Cameron Bancroft's explosive claims
articles.summary: Cameron Bancroft backed up Usman Khawaja's claims that the whole Australia team knew about the 2018 Sandpapergate, contradicting strong denials about it from Test captain Pat Cummins; Bancroft's lengthy statement added another twist to the ongoing scandal for Cricket Australia
articles.body:
Bancroft issued a 4,000-word statement on Wednesday insisting "the whole team" knew about plans to use sandpaper to tamper with the ball during the Test series against South Africa, supporting claims made by former team-mate Usman Khawaja .

The statement contradicts comments by Cummins during an extraordinary 68-minute press conference last week, where he forcefully denied renewed ball-tampering allegations, with Australian cricket rocked by conflicting reports from that series.

Cummins' management said on Wednesday there was "nothing in the [Bancroft's] statement that hasn't been answered", while Bancroft revealed last week's press conference was the "the final straw" in him deciding to speak out.

"I think that [statement] puts Cummins in a very difficult position," former England captain Nasser Hussain told Sky Sports News . "It's often not the crime, it's the cover-up that gets you. Finally, it looks like the truth is coming out from within that dressing room.

"I wouldn't be surprised if others came out [to speak] - they may take sides, but it was brave of Cameron Bancroft to come out and do what he's done.

"He's [Cummins] got some explaining to do because he was so strong. I was surprised he was so strong in his denial of what Usman Khawaja wrote in that book about the sandpaper scandal.

"Bancroft said himself that he felt betrayed and angry and alone after that press conference. If you're going to make that press conference 68 minutes, you better make sure everything you say is 100 per cent spot on."

'Cummins will have to talk about this again'

Bancroft was banned alongside then captain Steve Smith and David Warner in 2018, while his statement in the Western Australian newspaper revealed that Cummins' press conference comments made him 'feel angry, betrayed and alone'.

Cummins said he didn't want to answer questions again about that series after last week's press conference, although may be pressured into discussing it again after the latest fresh statements from past team-mates.

"He will probably have to [speak again] as Australia captain!" former England international Matt Prior told TNT Sports.

"His agent has come out with a statement to say he answered everything the other day, but he hasn't really because there's now new information that has come from Bancroft - there are a lot of question marks.

"There are coaches that need to stand up and be counted. This has completely opened this whole thing up. At what point do Cricket Australia not just owe to the public and to us as fans, but to the individuals whose lives were changed? They've got a responsibility to find out the truth.

"As much as everyone wants it to die down, it has become a big thing and you can't just brush it under the carpet."

On the statement itself and how Bancroft described the dressing room, Prior added: "If you ask me my experience in dressing rooms and how it goes on, whatever your plan is, whether ball swing or orthodox or reverse, that's the conversation that happens - everyone gets around (the table).

"The bowling coach is involved. The coach is involved. The bowlers are involved. The captain is involved. It's a team decision. That's why anyone that has been involved in cricket has found it really difficult to believe that the bowlers didn't know and no-one else knew.

"That statement, for me, actually screams of honesty."

How would the media manager know and not the bowlers?!

Bancroft gave a damaging account of conversations he had held with Cummins, Mithcell Starc and Josh Hazlewood during that 2018 Test, including the timeline of when sandpaper was used.

Cummins and the bowlers released a statement in 2021 denying they knew anything about the illegal tactic, reiterated by the Test captain last week, although Bancroft said more players knew and their media manager strongly objected using sandpaper.

"He [Cummins] could hide behind semantics and whether he knew sandpaper was being taken on the field that particular day or that particular session, but he directly said no," Hussain added.

"If you read the West Australian article from Bancroft, he says the media manager walked out because she was so unhappy with what was being discussed in a team meeting.

"How does the media manager know what's going on but a bowling unit doesn't? It would be the first time a bowling unit does not know what is happening to a cricket ball."

Will more players speak out on Sandpapergate?

The day began with Cricket Australia pledging to create an open forum for individuals to give their accounts of what happened, but former England captain Alastair Cook said that forum had been rendered "irrelevant" by Bancroft's statement.

"When Khawaja first came out, the first thing a lot of people thought was 'he's just selling a book'," Cook told TNT Sports.

"This one (the Bancroft statement) is an open, honest letter on his own accord, with clearly no financial gain to him about his experience of his eight-and-a-half years, and that's what's made me sit up (and listen).

"He's opened his own forum, hasn't he?" Cook said. "He has done it himself and hasn't allowed any administrator to get in the way of his words.

"It's the level of detail he has gone into and the level of detail that has gone into this statement, it has blown everything open. We had Cricket Australia this morning saying they have an open forum of safe spaces, but that is now irrelevant.

"It's another person telling his side of the story, that backs up three other players. We've not heard the end of it. Over the next 24-48 hours, it's all coming out - there's no doubt about that."

Australia play England in a five-match T20I series, beginning on Saturday in Melbourne, before further matches in Carrara (November 24), Brisbane (November 27), Sydney (November 29) and Canberra (December 2).

The Test side are next in action against New Zealand in Perth from December 9-13, with further Sandpapergate headlines likely in the days and weeks leading up to that four-match series.

articles.title: Kagiso Rabada's all-round show, Ryan Rickelton's ton put South Africa in command as Bangladesh crumble
articles.summary: Ryan Rickelton's century and Kagiso Rabada's all-round brilliance put South Africa in a commanding position against Bangladesh on Day 4 of the first Test
articles.body: Ryan Rickelton's century and Kagiso Rabada's all-round brilliance put South Africa in a commanding position against Bangladesh on Day 4 of the first Test at the Wanderers in Johannesburg on Wednesday.South Africa posted 557 to secure a 157-run first-innings lead, with Rickelton scoring 102 and Rabada producing his highest Test score of 72. The pair added 117 runs for the eighth wicket, while skipper Temba Bavuma contributed an unbeaten 68 despite returning after retiring hurt on the previous day. Dane Paterson chipped in with 29 as the hosts stretched their total beyond 550.Rickelton, who resumed on 56, reached his fourth Test century off 159 balls and eventually fell for 102 off 165 deliveries, hitting 13 fours. Rabada continued the assault after his dismissal, smashing two successive sixes off Mehidy Hasan Miraz before being stumped while attempting another.Bavuma and Paterson added 45 for the final wicket to take South Africa to 557, giving the hosts a substantial advantage.Bangladesh's second innings began poorly as they lost five wickets for 100 before bad light and rain forced an early close. With 28.4 overs still remaining, the visitors were 57 runs behind and facing an uphill battle to stay in the contest.Marco Jansen provided the first breakthrough, dismissing Tanzid Hasan Tamim for four before Rabada bowled Mominul Haque for one. Simon Harmer then removed Najmul Hossain Shanto for 11, catching him at first slip, before dismissing debutant Mahfijul Islam for 32.Islam battled for 92 deliveries before Harmer beat him through the gate. Rabada then dealt Bangladesh another blow, having first-innings centurion Towhid Hridoy caught behind for 23 with a sharp short ball after the batter had struck three consecutive boundaries.Rabada finished with two wickets, while Harmer also claimed two. Mushfiqur Rahim was unbeaten on five and Litton Das on 12 when the players left the field. Litton struck a six and a four off Harmer during a brief counter-attack.Earlier, Rabada's batting effort had given South Africa crucial lower-order runs. articles.body: Former England captain Nasser Hussain has questioned Australia's handling of the 2018 ball-tampering scandal, challenging Pat Cummins' denial of knowledge following fresh revelations from Cameron Bancroft. Hussain raised doubts over how members of the Australian bowling attack could have been unaware of the plan when the team's media manager reportedly knew about discussions surrounding the use of sandpaper.The controversy has resurfaced after Bancroft broke his silence on the infamous 'Sandpapergate' episode during Australia's 2018 tour of South Africa. The former opener admitted that he had withheld important details during Cricket Australia's initial investigation and suggested that knowledge of the plan extended beyond the three players who were sanctioned.Bancroft also expressed feeling "betrayed and alone" after Cummins publicly rejected former Australia batter Usman Khawaja's claims that the entire team knew about the ball-tampering plan.Nasser Hussain questions Cummins' denialReacting to Bancroft's latest revelations, Hussain questioned Cummins' claim that he had no knowledge of the ball-tampering plan. The former England skipper argued that the Australian captain's response during the press conference was direct and left little room for interpretation."Cummins said when directly asked the question: 'Were you aware of any ball tampering?' He said no," Hussain said, as quoted by Sky Sports."He could hide behind semantics and whether he knew sandpaper was being taken on the field that particular day or that particular session. But he directly said no."Hussain also referred to Bancroft's account of a team meeting, during which media manager Kate Hutchison reportedly walked out because she was uncomfortable with what was being discussed."If you read The West Australian article from Bancroft, he says the media manager walked out because she was so unhappy with what was being discussed in a team meeting.""How does the media manager know what's going on but a bowling unit does not? It would be the first time a bowling unit does not know what is happening to a cricket ball," he added.Hussain accuses Australia of leaving Smith, Warner and Bancroft to take the blameNasser also said that Bancroft, who faced a nine-month ban, and then captain and vice captain Steve Smith, who faced a year-long ban from all of cricket and immense public scrutiny in years to come, "took the bullet". He also slammed the Aussie team for their "un-Australian" way in which they left the aforementioned trio hanging, taking all the sanctions and public backlash."Those three [Bancroft, Warner, Smith], as Bancroft said, they took the bullet. And that is the thing. It is not the ball tampering - ball tampering has always happened in the history of cricket," he said."It is so un-Australian to have your three teammates and leave them hanging like that. To throw them under the bus like that.""It is just the whole mateship thing of Australia, the Baggy Green: 'We are all in this together.' And just to let three people take the blame," he continued.Nasser wondered how "incredibly difficult" the team environment must have been and why no one talked about "sticking together" as a team."I think out of everything in this terrible situation, the main thing is how an Australian team just moved on and let three people carry the can for what happened in Port Elizabeth and Cape Town," he signed off.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: India leave out Mohammed Siraj, Ravindra Jadeja; pick four-man pace attack for first New Zealand Test
articles.summary: India left out Mohammed Siraj despite opting for a four-man pace attack for the first Test against New Zealand at the Basin Reserve in Wellington on
articles.body: India left out Mohammed Siraj despite opting for a four-man pace attack for the first Test against New Zealand at the Basin Reserve in Wellington on Thursday. Captain Shubman Gill won the toss and elected to field, with Jasprit Bumrah leading a pace attack that also includes Akash Deep, Anshul Kamboj and Prasidh Krishna.Veteran all-rounder Ravindra Jadeja was another notable omission, with India preferring Washington Sundar as their spin-bowling option."We are going with four seamers with Akash Deep, Anshul Kamboj, Prasidh and Bumrah with Washington as the spinning all-rounder," Gill said at the toss."We were contemplating for the past one week which combination to, you know, go with because all of our fast bowlers have been doing really well. You know, very difficult for Siraj and Gurnoor for both of them to miss out. So it was a hard decision for us. But hopefully, all the fast bowlers that we picked, they should be able to do the job for us," the India skipper added.Reflecting on India's previous Test series in New Zealand, Gill stressed the importance of winning crucial moments during a match, warning that a team could quickly find itself in a difficult position even when the game appeared evenly balanced."I think it's very important to win some of the crucial moments in the game, you know. It might look like there's nothing much happening in the game. And then all of a sudden, you know, two, three wickets down. You know, suddenly too much behind in the game. So to be able to win those important moments, you know, that is very crucial for us," Gill said.Teams:India (Playing XI): KL Rahul, Yashasvi Jaiswal, Devdutt Padikkal, Shubman Gill(c), Rishabh Pant, Washington Sundar, Dhruv Jurel(w), Akash Deep, Anshul Kamboj, Jasprit Bumrah, Prasidh KrishnaNew Zealand (Playing XI): Tom Latham(c), Devon Conway, Henry Nicholls, Rachin Ravindra, Daryl Mitchell, Tom Blundell(w), Glenn Phillips, Nathan Smith, Kyle Jamieson, Matt Henry, Jacob DuffyGet the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Litton Das scripts history, Bangladesh keeper sets world record in South Africa Test
articles.summary: Bangladesh wicketkeeper Litton Das created a new world record for the most dismissals by a wicketkeeper in a single Test innings, taking his tally to
articles.body: Bangladesh wicketkeeper Litton Das created a new world record for the most dismissals by a wicketkeeper in a single Test innings, taking his tally to eight against South Africa in the ongoing first Test at the Wanderers in Johannesburg. He broke the record on the fourth morning when he stumped Kagiso Rabada, moving past the previous mark jointly held by five wicketkeepers.Wasim Bari, Bob Taylor, Ian Smith, Ridley Jacobs and Joshua Da Silva had all recorded seven dismissals in a Test innings. Da Silva was the last to achieve the feat, in 2023.Litton also became the first wicketkeeper to score a century and take eight dismissals in the same Test innings. Before him, Denis Lindsay in 1966 and AB de Villiers in 2013 had scored a hundred and taken six dismissals in an innings. Both had achieved the feat in Johannesburg.Litton had taken six catches by the end of the third day, dismissing Aiden Markram, Zubayr Hamza, Michael Breetzke, Wiaan Mulder, Marco Jansen and Simon Harmer. He added the stumpings of Ryan Rickelton and Rabada on the fourth morning to complete his record.Litton had also contributed with the bat in the first innings, scoring 120 off 179 balls, including 14 fours and a six. He shared a 206-run partnership for the sixth wicket with Towhid Hridoy as Bangladesh posted 400, their highest total against South Africa.Last month, Litton had recorded nine dismissals in a Test against Afghanistan, besides scoring a century and a half-century. He became the first wicketkeeper to achieve that combination in a Test and was named Player of the Match.The Bangladesh ODI and T20I captain is now at the top of the country's list of wicketkeepers with the most Test dismissals, having accounted for 154. Mushfiqur Rahim is second with 113.South Africa take control as Rickelton, Rabada lead the wayMeanwhile, South Africa took control of the first Test after Ryan Rickelton's century and an all-round contribution from Kagiso Rabada helped them build a first-innings lead of 157 runs.South Africa posted 557, with Rickelton scoring 102 and sharing a 117-run eighth-wicket partnership with Rabada, who made 72. Captain Temba Bavuma remained unbeaten on 68.Bangladesh struggled in their second innings and ended Day 4 at 100-5. Their troubles began after lunch when Marco Jansen dismissed Tanzid Hasan for four.Rabada then bowled Mominul Haque for one before Simon Harmer had Najmul Hossain Shanto caught at slip for 11. Harmer went on to bowl debutant opener Mahfijul Islam for 32, while Rabada removed first-innings centurion Towhid Hridoy, who was caught behind for 23.Mushfiqur Rahim, on five, and Litton Das, on 12, were at the crease when bad light and rain brought an early end to the day's play.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Gautam Gambhir's Kiwi Test: A defining red-ball challenge awaits India head coach in New Zealand
articles.summary: Few opponents have shaped Gautam Gambhir’s cricketing journey quite like New Zealand.
articles.body: Few opponents have shaped Gautam Gambhir’s cricketing journey quite like New Zealand. It was an ODI series in India vs the Black Caps in 20102011 where he first became India captain as MS Dhoni and Virender Sehwag were rested.It was against the Kiwis that he announced himself as one of India’s finest Test openers during the 2008-09 tour, scoring 445 runs in three Tests at an average of 89. His 137 and the 10-hour, 43-minute vigil in Napier in the second innings remains one of the most celebrated rescue acts by an Indian batter overseas and a masterclass in defensive batting that helped save a Test match and laid the foundation for a historic series victory.More than 15 years later, New Zealand continue to occupy a special place in Gambhir’s cricketing story, though not always for pleasant reasons. The Kiwis handed him the most embarrassing setback of his coaching tenure when they whitewashed India 3-0 at home in 2024, the first such defeat on Indian soil. Yet they were also the opponents India overcame in the Champions Trophy final in Dubai in 2025 and again in the T20 World Cup final earlier this year in Ahmedabad, victories that strengthened Gambhir’s reputation as a white-ball coach.On this sojourn, he has overseen series wins against New Zealand in both limited-overs formats. But Test cricket, the format Gambhir cherishes most, presents a completely different examination.The stakes could hardly be higher. India need victories in both Tests to remain firmly in contention for a place in the 2027 World Test Championship final.Having already missed out on the previous cycle’s final despite appearing favourites when Gambhir succeeded Rahul Dravid, another failure would inevitably raise uncomfortable questions about his red-ball credentials. That is where New Zealand present both a challenge and an opportunity.While Gambhir’s preference for multi-skilled cricketers has served India well in T20 cricket, the same philosophy has not always delivered in Tests.On more than one occasion, particularly overseas, India have appeared caught between strengthening the batting and maximising wickettaking options. Such hedging has robbed the side of the firepower needed to own the decisive moments.Team selection, therefore, could prove as important as execution.Communication between Gambhir and bowling coach Morne Morkel has been constant since the latter left the white-ball squad after the rain-hit ODI in Hamilton and travelled to Wellington to oversee preparations for the Test series.Asked about the attack at India’s disposal, Morkel’s message to the head coach was definitive.“My feedback to Gautam was that we have enough in attack to take 20 wickets.”That belief could shape India’s selections over the next two weeks.Despite being one of the architects of India’s T20 revolution through the 2007 World Cup triumph, Gambhir remains deeply old-school in his cricketing outlook.In an era when youngsters romanticise about an IPL gig more than an India cap, he continues to view Ranji Trophy as the ideal finishing school and Test cricket as the ultimate dipstick to measure a player and team’s worth. It is a philosophy he has repeatedly articulated.Success in the longest format, he believes, leaves the deepest imprint and defines legacies. New Zealand now offers him the chance to reinforce that belief.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Tom Latham equals Virender Sehwag in unwanted batting record list after first over duck against India
articles.summary: New Zealand captain Tom Latham was dismissed for a duck against India in the first Test of the two-match series at the Basin Reserve in Wellington on
articles.body: New Zealand captain Tom Latham was dismissed for a duck against India in the first Test of the two-match series at the Basin Reserve in Wellington on Thursday, November 19. Jasprit Bumrah bowled the left-handed opener with the third ball of the match after India captain Shubman Gill won the toss and elected to field.Latham's dismissal put him on an unwanted list of New Zealand captains. He became only the fourth Kiwi skipper to be dismissed for a duck in a home Test against India. Barry Sinclair was the first, while Stephen Fleming was the last to suffer the same fate before Latham. Fleming had scored a three-ball duck in the first innings of the January 1999 Test at Seddon Park in Hamilton.The 34-year-old also equalled former India opener Virender Sehwag in the record for the most ducks by an opener in Test cricket. Latham has now been dismissed without scoring 15 times as an opener.Most ducks as an opener in Test cricket19 - Kraigg Brathwaite17 - Mike Atherton16 - Marvan Atapattu15 - Virender Sehwag15 - Tom LathamBumrah marks return with three wicketsBumrah made an immediate impact on his return to international cricket, taking three wickets as India reduced New Zealand to 70/5 after lunch on the opening day. The 32-year-old pacer had been out of action for India since the second Test against South Africa in November last year, mainly because of injury.New Zealand have been Bumrah's most difficult opponent in Test cricket in terms of his bowling average. While he has taken 52 Tests to build an overall average of 19.79, his nine wickets in five Tests against New Zealand have come at an average of 45.44.Bumrah began his spell with the new ball after Gill elected to bowl on a green pitch. Bowling over the wicket, he pitched the ball around off stump to Latham, who chose to leave it, expecting it to move away. The delivery straightened and hit the top of off stump, giving India an early breakthrough.Bumrah returned for a second spell before lunch and dismissed Daryl Mitchell. The batter had tried to counter the pacer by stepping down the pitch. Gill responded by placing a fielder close on the leg side, and the move paid off. Mitchell (1) edged the ball onto his pad before it carried to Yashasvi Jaiswal, who took the catch.Bumrah struck again after lunch, having Tom Blundell caught by Gill at first slip. The wicket was his third of the innings. At the time of writing New Zealand were 117/5 in 43 overs.FOLLOW LIVEGet the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Jasprit Bumrah's moment of reckoning: India's pace spearhead faces defining Test challenge in New Zealand
articles.summary: Jasprit Bumrah has built a career on delivering when India need him most.
articles.body: Jasprit Bumrah has built a career on delivering when India need him most. Yet as Shubman Gill’s men begin a crucial two-Test series against New Zealand on Nov 19, the world’s premier fast bowler finds himself facing an unusual challenge: proving his worth in the format he values above all else.The numbers present a curious contradiction. Against the six other Test-playing nations he has bowled to — Australia (17.15), Bangladesh (12.81), England (22.89), South Africa (20.36), Sri Lanka (9) and West Indies (13.1) — Bumrah averages a surreal 18.76. Against New Zealand, however, that figure climbs to 45.44 from five Tests. The strike-rate too is a high 92.8. For a bowler who has conquered conditions and opponents around the world, New Zealand remains one of the few unfinished chapters in an otherwise extraordinary career.Bumrah’s last bowling effort in a Test came against South Africa on Day Four in Guwahati on Nov 25, 2025, 358 days ago. Since then, India have carefully managed his workload. The strategy has been designed to extend the career of a fast bowler with an unconventional action and a history of injuries, but it has also invited scrutiny. The criticism gathered momentum this year.Bumrah played through a niggle during the IPL and looked unusually short of his best. He did not play in the third ODI at Lord’s due to injury and missed the Sri Lanka tour. His stature, however, remains intact. He played starring roles in India’s T20 World Cup triumphs in 2024 and 2026 and continued to be the team’s biggest wickettaking threat whenever fit.In Australia during the BorderGavaskar Trophy in 2024-25, he once again showed his class before suffering an injury in the final Test in Sydney. The knock-on effect was evident in England, where India chose to play him in only three of the five Tests. He claimed five-wicket hauls in Leeds and at Lord’s, but India lost both matches. In Leeds, one felt he did not bowl enough in the second innings, when the game was in the balance. At Old Trafford, his pace dipped in the second innings and he was rested for the final Test at the Oval, where Mohammed Siraj did Mohammed Siraj things.As a result, questions resurfaced. Ex-players, critics and fans have wondered whether India can afford to manage their premier bowler so conservatively. Some have accused him of picking and choosing games. Others believe workload management has come at the cost of impact in the longest format.New Zealand could be the perfect place for a response. India arrive at the Basin needing a win here, as well as in the second Test in Christchurch, to keep their World Test Championship (WTC) ambitions firmly on track. The conditions are expected to favour fast bowlers and, after months of careful planning, Bumrah is rested, fresh and ready. Is he rusty, though?Bowling coach Morne Morkel dismissed concerns over Bumrah’s preparations. “I wouldn’t say he bowled less. He bowled on back-toback days and spent long spells bowling to batters in the nets. Two days before a game, we generally like to give bowlers time off their feet to get mentally ready. He did a lot of overs in the nets and a lot of work preparing for this Test. But you also need to trust an experienced player in terms of how he gets ready,” he said.Significantly, Morkel made it clear that India will need their fast bowlers, senior or junior, to go beyond their comfort zones if they are to reach the WTC final. “For us to play in that final, we need to push ourselves harder, take ourselves a little bit more out of our comfort zone. If the opportunity is crying out for a guy to bowl an extra two or three overs, that’s going to be needed,” Morkel said.Nov 19 is a date that evokes painful memories for Indian cricket fans. On this day in 2023, India lost the World Cup final to Australia despite a threatening opening spell from Bumrah. As another Nov 19 arrives, India face a nation that has repeatedly blocked their path in global events, from the 2019 World Cup semifinal to the 2021 World Test Championship final. Bumrah featured in all those defeats. Two Tests in New Zealand now offer him a chance to flip the narrative.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Sandpapergate deepens: Pat Cummins under pressure as Cameron Bancroft's explosive claims trigger calls for captaincy review
articles.summary: Australia captain Pat Cummins is facing mounting pressure over his leadership following Cameron Bancroft's explosive revelations about the 2018
articles.body: Australia captain Pat Cummins is facing mounting pressure over his leadership following Cameron Bancroft's explosive revelations about the 2018 ball-tampering scandal, with calls growing for an immediate review of his position as Test skipper.Bancroft, who was banned for nine months for his role in the infamous 'Sandpapergate' scandal, has questioned Cummins' credibility over his repeated denials of knowledge of the ball-tampering plot, claiming the captain's recent comments were the "final straw" that prompted him to break his silence.The 33-year-old also revealed that speaking publicly about the incident had left him feeling relieved and liberated after carrying the burden for years. In an explosive 4,497-word column published on Wednesday, Bancroft reiterated claims that the wider Australian team was aware of the plan to tamper with the ball during the 2018 South Africa tour."Obviously, yeah, I’ve been carrying a lot of this stuff for a long period of time," Bancroft said after releasing his account, as per 9News in Perth."So I feel really freed and really happy to be able to do that. And obviously now there’s a process in place which Cricket Australia have put in (forum). Yeah, I look forward to being a part of that process," he added.Cummins' denial comes under fresh scrutinyCummins, however, has stood firm on his position that he had no knowledge of the ball-tampering plan, maintaining that his account of the events has remained consistent over the past eight years.His manager Neil Maxwell issued a statement reiterating the Australian captain's stance, while expressing sympathy for Bancroft."Pat's position hasn't changed in eight years. He's been consistent and adamant from day one," Maxwell said."Pat feels for Cam (Bancroft) of course. He has been through a lot. We would urge people to again read Pat's interview transcript. There is nothing he hasn't answered. And that includes in response to what Cam has now said."The developments have nevertheless intensified scrutiny of Cummins' leadership, with prominent Australian cricket writer Robert Craddock calling for an immediate review of his captaincy."Pat Cummins' future as test captain should be placed under immediate review after Cameron Bancroft's stunning accusation that the skipper didn't tell us the truth," Craddock wrote in The Australian.The growing controversy has also prompted questions across Australian media about whether Cummins can continue as Test captain amid the renewed scrutiny surrounding the scandal.Bancroft's account reopens old woundsIn his latest account, Bancroft acknowledged that David Warner had raised the idea of using sandpaper on the ball to generate reverse swing during the second Test against South Africa in Port Elizabeth in 2018.The discussion reportedly took place during the tea break on Day 2, in the presence of bowling coach David Saker and then head coach Darren Lehmann.The revelations have reopened wounds from the Cape Town Test, where Bancroft was caught using sandpaper on the ball. The incident resulted in lengthy bans for Bancroft, Warner and then-captain Steve Smith, who was also stripped of the captaincy.The controversy resurfaced following Usman Khawaja's allegations in his autobiography that the wider team knew about the plan and should collectively accept responsibility. Warner and former Australia pacer Chadd Sayers have also backed Khawaja's account, adding to the pressure on Cricket Australia (CA).CA's 2018 investigation had concluded that the conspiracy was limited to the three players who were punished.Cricket Australia opens independent forumAmid the renewed controversy, CA chief executive Todd Greenberg announced the establishment of an independent forum to allow players to share their accounts of the scandal.However, Greenberg made it clear that the governing body was not looking to reopen the investigation or impose fresh sanctions."Looking for the perfect truth doesn't exist, and we're not chasing that," Greenberg told reporters on Wednesday.Former Australia opener Warner, meanwhile, appeared reluctant to revisit the episode, saying he had nothing further to add when asked whether he would participate in the forum."At the end of the day, we owned what we did. So we can't do any more," Warner told the media in Sydney.Sayers was also uncertain about participating, questioning the usefulness of a process that might not make the complete accounts public."What's the point ... if there's certain bits that they want to cut out," he told local radio station SEN on Thursday.With Bancroft now willing to participate in CA's independent process and fresh questions being raised about what the wider group knew, Sandpapergate has once again become a major issue for Australian cricket. For Cummins, whose denial remains unchanged, the controversy has evolved into an increasingly uncomfortable test of his leadership.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 'You haven't picked him': Sunil Gavaskar questions Mohammed Siraj's omission, says pacer has 'never let India down'
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: India's decision to leave Mohammed Siraj out of the playing XI for the first Test against New Zealand in Wellington did not go down well with
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India's decision to leave Mohammed Siraj out of the playing XI for the first Test against New Zealand in Wellington did not go down well with Sunil Gavaskar. The former India captain was surprised that an experienced bowler like Siraj was not considered among India's top four pacers.India went into the Test with Jasprit Bumrah, Akash Deep, Anshul Kamboj and Prasidh Krishna as their four fast bowlers. Washington Sundar was picked as the spin-bowling all-rounder.The decision came under the scanner as New Zealand fought back in the second session on Thursday. After losing four wickets for 60 runs in the first session, the hosts reached 214/5 by the end of the 70th over. Henry Nicholls scored a century, while Glenn Phillips was closing in on one.Bumrah picked up three wickets, while Kamboj and Akash Deep took one each. Prasidh Krishna went wicketless.'Siraj has never let India down': Gavaskar questions selectionSpeaking on Sony Sports after the toss, Gavaskar said he was surprised by Siraj's omission. He also said the fast bowler had done nothing wrong to lose his place in the team."There were signs when he did not join the Test squad early. I thought they were going to play him after he featured in the final ODI. But this is a surprise. I don't think he has let India down. He has never let India down," Gavaskar said."There is nothing wrong with his bowling. His rhythm is good. He has been fine, from what I have observed of the cricket he has played recently. Why he has not been picked is something I don't know. I only hope the others who have been picked ahead of him deliver."Gavaskar questioned the decision again after the second session. He pointed out that Kamboj and Prasidh had much less Test experience than Siraj."Anshul Kamboj and Prasidh Krishna started playing Tests only a year or two ago. On the other hand, Mohammed Siraj, one of your experienced bowlers, was available and you haven't picked him. For me, to think Siraj is not among your top four bowlers is a little hard to get over. I'm not saying he would have got you wickets, but the way they batted, the fact of the matter is that when you don't have that experience... Look, it all looks very good, the figures, the economy rate, the ball is moving and they're bowling wide of the stumps, so the batters are leaving and the economy looks good."They did very well in the first session, but if they had got more wickets immediately after that, it would have been a different story," Gavaskar said.Kamboj made his Test debut in 2025, while Prasidh played his first Test in 2023.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Henry Nicholls joins Kane Williamson, Martin Crowe in elite list with century against India
articles.summary: Henry Nicholls took 188 balls to score a century for New Zealand in the first innings of the ongoing first Test against India at Basin Reserve in
articles.body: Henry Nicholls took 188 balls to score a century for New Zealand in the first innings of the ongoing first Test against India at Basin Reserve in Wellington on Thursday (November 19). The left-handed batter reached the milestone by taking a single off the second ball of the 70th over, registering his fifth Test century at the venue.With this, Nicholls has equalled Martin Crowe and Kane Williamson's record for the most Test centuries by a New Zealand batter at Basin Reserve. All three have scored five centuries at the ground. Nicholls has also become the sixth player in the world to score more than 1,000 Test runs at the venue.Williamson, New Zealand's highest run-scorer in Test cricket, played 18 Tests at Basin Reserve between 2011 and 2025, scoring five centuries. Former captain Crowe also scored five centuries in 10 Tests at the venue during his career.Most Test hundreds for NZ at a venue7 - Kane Williamson - Seddon Park, Hamilton (21 inns)6 - Ross Taylor - Seddon Park, Hamilton (24 inns)5 - Henry Nicholls - Basin Reserve, Wellington (15 inns)5 - Martin Crowe - Basin Reserve, Wellington (17 inns)5 - Kane Williamson - Basin Reserve, Wellington (30 inns)Williamson holds the record for the most Test centuries by a New Zealand batter at a single venue. He scored seven centuries in 12 Tests at Seddon Park in Hamilton. Ross Taylor is next on the list, with six centuries in 13 Tests at the same ground.The world record for the most Test centuries at a single venue belongs to Mahela Jayawardene. The former Sri Lanka batter scored 11 centuries in 27 Tests at the Sinhalese Sports Club Ground in Colombo between 1997 and 2014.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Just when India needed a breakthrough to break New Zealand's growing partnership, they missed a big chance in the first Test at the Basin
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Just when India needed a breakthrough to break New Zealand's growing partnership, they missed a big chance in the first Test at the Basin Reserve in Wellington on Thursday.Henry Nicholls and Glenn Phillips had put together a partnership of more than 150 runs and were making life difficult for the Indian bowlers. However, India got an opportunity to break the stand in the 74th over when Nicholls mistimed a pull shot off Prasidh Krishna.The ball went high in the air towards backward square leg, where Devdutt Padikkal was waiting. But wicketkeeper Rishabh Pant also ran towards the ball, leading to confusion between the two fielders.Padikkal initially hesitated as Pant came into his line of sight. Pant also slowed down before realising that Padikkal was better placed to take the catch. By the time Padikkal stretched his hands, it was too late. He got his fingertips to the ball but could not hold on.Prasidh was left in disbelief and covered his mouth with his hand. Padikkal and Pant also looked disappointed, while India captain Shubman Gill was visibly unhappy with the missed chance.It was a costly miss for India as Nicholls got another opportunity to continue his innings and New Zealand's fightback.Bumrah strikes three times as India reduce NZ to 70/5India had started well after Gill won the toss and elected to bowl. Jasprit Bumrah and Anshul Kamboj reduced New Zealand to 12/2 early in the innings.Bumrah dismissed New Zealand captain Tom Latham for a duck, while Kamboj sent back Devon Conway for four.Henry Nicholls and Rachin Ravindra then tried to steady the innings and took the hosts to 50 in 18.2 overs. However, Akash Deep broke the partnership in the following over by dismissing Ravindra for 15.Bumrah struck again just before lunch, removing Daryl Mitchell for one. He then dismissed wicketkeeper-batter Tom Blundell for five in the second session.Bumrah had three wickets to his name, while Kamboj and Akash Deep picked up one each.New Zealand were struggling at 70/5 at one stage, but Nicholls and Phillips fought back with a big partnership. articles.title: Strange fate of a 'captain's dream': India's decision to drop Mohammed Siraj makes little sense
articles.summary: Mohammed Siraj does not get to play in T20Is, is no longer a regular in India's ODI side, and now, even in the format where he has been most convincing,
articles.body: Mohammed Siraj does not get to play in T20Is, is no longer a regular in India's ODI side, and now, even in the format where he has been most convincing, the Indian pacer has been left out of the playing XI. The last time Siraj played a Test in a SENA country was at The Oval in August 2025, where he took nine wickets in the match to help India secure a famous victory and level the series against England. In Wellington, however, India have left out their second-best fast bowler in Test cricket over the last few years. It is difficult to understand the reasoning behind the team management's decision.After the victory at The Oval, Shubman Gill had called Siraj a “captain’s dream”. At the toss in Wellington, the India skipper admitted that leaving him out was a "hard decision". But acknowledging how difficult a selection call was does not necessarily explain why it was made.Siraj has taken 144 wickets in 48 Tests, with 108 of them coming in away or neutral venues. He has become the bowler India can turn to when the ball is not moving, or there is little or no help from the wicket. He has done that alongside Jasprit Bumrah and, at times, in his absence. His value to the team goes beyond his wicket tally. His contribution has not just been about the wickets. Siraj has put his body on the line, bowled long spells and kept coming back because that is what the team needed.What makes his omission harder to understand is that the uncertainty around his place is not limited to one format. He has not played T20Is regularly, his ODI opportunities have been sporadic, and now his place in the Test side also appears dispensable. Siraj has spoken about how regular bowling helps him find his rhythm, saying that the more he bowls, the better he feels.Fast bowling depends on rhythm, repetition and confidence. Keeping a bowler like Siraj, who has been a mainstay of India's attack, in and out of the side does not necessarily help him find any of those things.The reasons behind his exclusion are also difficult to justify. Gill said before the match that India would play four pacers “for sure” and indicated that Kamboj and Akash Deep or Nitish Reddy could make the XI because of their batting ability. Between Kamboj and Nitish Reddy, Kamboj was clearly the better choice as a specialist bowler who can contribute with the bat, rather than a batter who bowls occasionally.India's final combination in Wellington makes Siraj's omission even harder to defend. Washington Sundar was already in the XI as the all-rounder, while the choice between Akash Deep and Anshul Kamboj was a reasonable one. Kamboj offers something with the bat, but he is also a specialist bowler. Picking one of the two would have given India another seam option without affecting the balance of the side.Instead, India selected both and left Siraj out. The Basin Reserve had a green surface, and India had won the toss and elected to bowl. The team wanted to make use of the conditions, yet left out one of their bowling mainstay.As Gill explained at the toss, leaving Siraj out was a combination call. India chose to provide some additional batting cover at the expense of a strike bowler. That is a questionable trade-off in any Test, but even more so against a New Zealand side that India have not beaten in a Test while touring the country since 2009.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Jasprit Bumrah fights alone as India's Siraj-less pace attack lets New Zealand off the hook on day 1
articles.summary: Jasprit Bumrah was the only Indian pacer who consistently troubled New Zealand's batters on day 1 of the first Test at the Basin Reserve in Wellington on
articles.body: Jasprit Bumrah was the only Indian pacer who consistently troubled New Zealand's batters on day 1 of the first Test at the Basin Reserve in Wellington on Thursday. While Bumrah took three wickets, his pace-bowling partners struggled to make an impact as Henry Nicholls and Glenn Phillips put New Zealand in control with an unbeaten 173-run partnership for the sixth wicket.New Zealand were reduced to 70 for 5 after India won the toss and elected to bowl. However, Nicholls (113 not out off 221 balls) and Phillips (94 not out off 181 balls) turned the innings around, taking the hosts to 243 for 5 at stumps. Nicholls completed his 12th Test century, while Phillips was six runs short of his hundred.Bumrah finished the day with figures of 3/52 in 17 overs. When he had Tom Blundell (5) caught by Shubman Gill at slip, India had a chance to bowl New Zealand out for a low total. But the other Indian pacers could not build on his effort. The Kookaburra ball also began losing its shine after the 30th over, making it harder for the bowlers to generate movement.Anshul Kamboj (1/57 in 18 overs), nicknamed 'AK-47', picked up an early wicket but struggled thereafter. Kamboj's restrictive, wicket-to-wicket approach did not bring him further success. Prasidh Krishna (0/58 in 16 overs), meanwhile, conceded boundaries while repeatedly bowling either too full or too short.Akash Deep (1/33 in 16 overs) had some good spells, but Bumrah remained biggest threat for New Zealand batters even after the ball had lost its shine. He beat Nicholls' bat on several occasions but could not get another wicket. New Zealand began to recover after lunch, with Phillips taking the attack to the Indian bowlers and allowing Nicholls to settle into his innings.Nicholls took 188 balls to reach his hundred, using cover drives and shots through mid-wicket to score his runs. Phillips was more attacking at the other end, and the boundaries came more frequently as the partnership progressed.Kamboj's lack of pace was also a factor, with his deliveries often allowing the batters to play without taking much risk. His average speed was around 128 to 130 kmph, which made it difficult for him to trouble the New Zealand batters once the conditions eased.ALSO READ: Strange fate of a 'captain's dream' - India's decision to drop Mohammed Siraj makes little senseAfter Nicholls completed his 12th Test century, Prasidh nearly dismissed him with a short ball that he attempted to hook. However, a misunderstanding between wicketkeeper Rishabh Pant and Devdutt Padikkal meant the latter misjudged the catch.Earlier, Gill had won the toss and Bumrah received support from the other end while the new Kookaburra ball still had its shine. New Zealand lost captain Tom Latham (0), Conway (4), Rachin Ravindra (15) and Daryl Mitchell (1) in the morning session.Bumrah dismissed Latham with the third ball of the match. The New Zealand captain left the delivery, expecting it to move away with the angle, but the ball came back in and hit the off-bail.Mitchell, meanwhile, tried to counter the bounce and movement by stepping forward after arriving at the crease. Bumrah asked Gill to keep a short-leg fielder, and the move brought an immediate result. Mitchell stepped out again and was struck by a delivery around waist height. He attempted to whip it away, but Yashasvi Jaiswal took the catch at short leg.Bumrah then dismissed Blundell by repeatedly bowling at the same spot before pulling his length back by a foot. The change squared up the New Zealand batter, who edged the ball to Gill at slip. That proved to be India's last wicket of the day.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Mohammed Siraj snub under scanner as India pacers struggle! Kotak defends team selection after New Zealand fightback in 1st Test
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: India batting coach Sitanshu Kotak defended the decision to leave Mohammed Siraj out of the playing XI for the first Test against New Zealand,
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India batting coach Sitanshu Kotak defended the decision to leave Mohammed Siraj out of the playing XI for the first Test against New Zealand, insisting that the selectors and team management had picked the best possible combination despite the pacer's omission coming under scrutiny after a difficult opening day for India's bowling attack at the Basin Reserve in Wellington on Thursday.With Jasprit Bumrah doing most of the damage, India's other pace options struggled to make an impact as New Zealand recovered from 70/5 to reach 243/5 at stumps. Henry Nicholls remained unbeaten on 113, while Glenn Phillips was six runs short of a century at 94 not out, the pair putting together an unbroken 173-run stand for the sixth wicket.Siraj's absence was particularly noticeable as Anshul Kamboj, playing in his place, managed just one wicket for 57 runs in 18 overs. Prasidh Krishna went wicketless, conceding 58 runs in 16 overs, while Akash Deep returned figures of 1/33. Bumrah, meanwhile, finished with 3/52 from 17 overs.Kotak explains why Siraj was left outAsked about Siraj's omission at the post-day press conference, Kotak backed the selection call and said the team management had considered the conditions and opposition while settling on its best XI."I think at a time they pick the team, they think about the best XI, and that’s what played. Nothing wrong with Siraj, they thought of the best possible XI and played. Sri Lanka was different conditions. Not wrong decision to drop Siraj," Kotak said.He also explained the thinking behind India's bowling combination, pointing to the different skills offered by the pace attack and the decision to include Washington Sundar because New Zealand had four left-handers in their XI."On current attack: Two bowlers swing the ball well and two seam the ball well. And have pace. When you pick XI, you think about all days. Picked Washi because of four left-handers in opposition XI," he added.The decision, however, came under the spotlight as Bumrah repeatedly troubled the New Zealand batters while the other Indian bowlers struggled to maintain pressure after the new ball lost its shine.'Prasidh is an attacking bowler'Kotak also defended Prasidh, whose expensive spell included several boundary-scoring deliveries, saying the Karnataka pacer was an attacking option who could be expensive while searching for wickets."Prasidh is an attacking bowler and he can go for runs. People like it when he picks wickets, and they don’t when they go for runs," Kotak said.India had made an impressive start after winning the toss, with Bumrah removing Tom Latham, Devon Conway and Daryl Mitchell before dismissing Tom Blundell to reduce the hosts to 70/5. Kamboj also struck early, but Nicholls and Phillips turned the contest around with a patient yet increasingly assured partnership.Kotak felt India had an opportunity to make further inroads, particularly with a chance to dismiss Nicholls going down."The pitch helped with the new ball, the weather was good and sunny so it dried out. We should have taken that catch, Rishabh Pant went for the catch but it was close to Devdutt Padikkal," he said.Nicholls eventually reached his 12th Test century, while Phillips continued to counter-attack as India's bowling attack lost its early bite. Bumrah was the only bowler who consistently threatened, leaving India with plenty to ponder after surrendering control of a day that had begun so promisingly.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Cameron Bancroft: Former Australia batter says he feels 'very free' after 'telling the truth' with Sandpapergate claims
articles.summary: Cameron Bancroft says he "never meant to point fingers or implicate others; "I just wanted to, for my own peace, to tell the truth;" in making his statement on the 2018 ball tampering scandal; meanwhile, Pat Cummins' manager says Test captain has been "consistent and adamant from day one"
articles.body:
In a 4,000-word statement in The West Australian newspaper on Wednesday, Bancroft broke his silence on revelations in Usman Khawaja's new book, claiming that Cummins' press conference denying the allegations was the "final straw" for him, revealing that the entire bowling unit maintained full knowledge of the extensive use of sandpaper.

Bancroft saw his career turned upside after being suspended for his part in the 2018 incident alongside then captain Steve Smith and vice-captain David Warner. Those were the only three players to be punished.

Speaking to local media on Thursday, Bancroft said: "I never meant to point fingers or implicate others; I just wanted to, for my own peace, to tell the truth.

"This has been a burden that I've carried with me for such a long period of time but I feel very free and I feel very happy that I've been able to do that."

Footage on social media on Thursday also showed Cummins being approached for comment by local TV reporters when leaving his house for training with New South Wales. The Australian Test captain declined to address Bancroft's remarks.

A statement from his manager, Neil Maxwell, said: "Pat's position hasn't changed in eight years. He's been consistent and adamant from day one.

"Pat feels for Cam [Bancroft] of course. He has been through a lot. We would urge people to again read Pat's interview transcript. There is nothing he hasn't answered. And that includes in response to what Cam has now said."

Bancroft's statement has heaped pressure on Test captain Cummins, with Australia's next red-ball series against New Zealand beginning on December 9.

The claims come in the wake of a furore of discussion around the 2018 scandal, with Khawaja's book first bringing to light claims that the entire team knew about the use of sandpaper.

Khawaja also alleged that discussions about ball-tampering had been held "openly and lightheartedly" across the entire squad, involving not just the batters, bowlers and coaching staff but the wider team.

Cummins dismissed Khawaja's claims as "complete and utter nonsense" during a sensational 68-minute press conference last Friday.

articles.title: 'It'd be great if you could be the first': Groundsman's wish comes true as Henry Nicholls hits ton vs India
articles.summary: Henry Nicholls shared a light-hearted moment with the Basin Reserve groundsman before the first Test against India.
articles.body: Henry Nicholls shared a light-hearted moment with the Basin Reserve groundsman before the first Test against India. The New Zealand batter joked about scoring a century at the venue. He went on to do exactly that, finishing the opening day in Wellington unbeaten on 113 on Thursday.Nicholls played a key role in New Zealand's recovery after India reduced them to 60/4 at Lunch and then 70/5. He joined Glenn Phillips in the middle and the two added an unbeaten 173 runs for the sixth wicket to take New Zealand to 243/5 at stumps. Phillips was also close to a century, remaining unbeaten on 94 off 182 balls.India's fast bowlers had made good use of the conditions early in the day, but Nicholls and Phillips showed patience and put the hosts back in a strong position.Nicholls' banter with groundsmanSpeaking after the day's play, Nicholls talked about his special connection with the Basin Reserve.Five of his 12 Test centuries have come at this venue. He also revealed an interesting conversation with the groundsman before the match."Yeah, I'm not sure. I was having a bit of banter with the groundsman. He was saying it's his first time, first year here and he said that the first game, or the second game, I scored the first hundred here. So he said this morning, he said, oh, it'd be great if you could be the first. And I said, oh, before the toss, I said, oh yeah, maybe tomorrow or later on. But yeah, I mean it's, it's a special place to play. I think anyone who's a cricket fan or plays cricket loves playing at the Basin and that's certainly, for me, is a traditional ground and it's a lot of history here. So yeah, so to have that many here is pretty special," Nicholls said.The left-handed batter has now scored five centuries and four half-centuries in just 15 Test innings at the Basin Reserve.Among New Zealand players, only Kane Williamson, with seven centuries at Seddon Park, and Ross Taylor, with six at the same venue, have scored more Test hundreds at a single ground.'His energy is infectious': Nicholls on partnership with PhillipsNicholls also praised Phillips for his role in New Zealand's fightback. The pair put the Indian bowlers under pressure with their 173-run partnership."Yeah, I mean his energy is infectious, the way he came out. I guess put a bit more pressure on them probably allowed me just to go about my work. And really enjoyed batting with him. A couple of guys who love running really hard and putting a bit of pressure on the Indian side that way. So, he batted fantastically and like I say for us to both be not out certainly a boost for the dressing room," he said.Nicholls also spoke about the special feeling of having his family at the ground. His wife Lucy was celebrating her birthday on Thursday."Yeah, it was really awesome. You know, even the non-strikers' end, I'm just looking up and seeing the kids playing up there. And yeah, it's my wife's birthday today as well, shout out to Lucy, she's the rock and it was pretty cool to have them. My mum and dad were there as well. So just, yeah, a really special day."Nicholls happy with New Zealand's fightbackNicholls admitted that India's bowlers made life difficult for New Zealand after the early loss of wickets. However, he was pleased with the way the team fought back and ended the day on a strong note."Um, yeah, I don't know. It's obviously, it's still pretty fresh to be honest. But yeah, it was really nice. I guess the position we're in to have that partnership with Glenn and I guess for us to both be there at the end of the day is even more pleasing."Yeah, I was sort of rushing a little bit to get ready to the top to be honest. But yeah, I mean obviously they bowled incredibly well and we know when we play here that that can be the challenge when you lose the toss and get put in. But I think all the guys worked really hard and it was just nice to have that partnership from the middle session right through the end of the day," he said.New Zealand's recovery also added to a rare trend in Test cricket. There have been 31 instances of teams putting together sixth-wicket partnerships of 150 or more after losing their first five wickets for fewer than 100 runs.India have now conceded six such partnerships, including the ongoing stand between Nicholls and Phillips. This is the joint-highest number alongside New Zealand.The biggest sixth-wicket partnership in this situation remains the 352-run stand between Brendon McCullum and BJ Watling at the Basin Reserve in 2014. articles.title: 'Cummins will struggle to captain Australia': Ian Healy's blunt warning after Bancroft's Sandpapergate revelations
articles.summary: Former Australia wicketkeeper Ian Healy has warned that Pat Cummins will struggle to lead the Test side unless he directly refutes Cameron Bancroft’s
articles.body: Former Australia wicketkeeper Ian Healy has warned that Pat Cummins will struggle to lead the Test side unless he directly refutes Cameron Bancroft’s explosive claim that the entire team knew about the ball-tampering plan during the infamous 2018 Cape Town Test.Bancroft, one of the central figures in the Sandpapergate scandal, said on Tuesday that the entire team was aware of the conspiracy but he ended up taking "the bullet" for everyone. His remarks have reignited questions over what happened in South Africa and the credibility of those who maintained they knew nothing about the plot.The latest controversy follows Cummins dismissing former teammate Usman Khawaja's claim in his book that the entire team knew about the ball-tampering plan as “complete and utter nonsense.”Reacting to Bancroft's fresh allegations, Healy said Cummins needed to address the issue directly if he wanted to retain his authority as captain."I would feel without refuting Cameron Bancroft's words again, he (Cummins) will struggle to captain the team.“You've had a big part of your credibility taken away with that press conference now that it's been proven to be not as complete as Pat made it out to be,” Healy told SEN.ALSO READ: Cummins under pressure as Bancroft's explosive claims trigger calls for captaincy reviewHealy says Cummins need not step downAsked whether Cummins should stand down as Australia captain, Healy said he did not believe that was necessary, while questioning the way Cricket Australia had handled the scandal in 2018."No, he doesn't need to stand down. And I don't want to get into another panic mode of what happened in 2018, it was panic, and they tried to do an investigation in no time, didn't talk to anyone, it was rubbish. It was a lack of quality and rubbish, and rushed, and panicked."Now, I can't say whether he should stand down now. Will he stand down? That might be a different thing. He might stand down," said the 62-year-old, who played 119 Tests and 168 ODIs between 1988 and 1999.Healy also argued that the latest revelations could damage the personal legacies of Cummins and fellow Australia bowlers Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc and Nathan Lyon, who had said they were unaware of the ball-tampering plan.“I would say it taints their personal legacies. I don't think it's going to taint their performance legacies. Personally now, they're not as credible as they once were, unless they change something drastically in the next few days," Healy said.Healy also suggested that the ball-tampering could have been happening for longer than previously believed.“So they probably achieved some success with their skills, with a ball that's doing more than it was going to. That's a little bit of a part of their career legacy," he added.Healy calls for Lehmann to speak, rules out fresh probeHealy believes former Australia coach Darren Lehmann should now disclose what he knows about the scandal."If he's going to do it, now's the time. But I think the dots have been joined there too. It was an ugly underbelly with an average attitude, and he was in charge of it,” Healy said.Healy also accused Cricket Australia of orchestrating a cover-up in the aftermath of the scandal, arguing that the panic following the events in South Africa resulted in a flawed investigation.“Yes, I think so...the panic and the chaos back here in Australia - they had no idea about it in South Africa - it was unbelievably emotional and led to a poor quality investigation which might have been covering up a motivation not to get everyone sacked," he said.However, Healy does not believe Cricket Australia should reopen the investigation.“No. I don't think there's any value in it. The dots are joining for us now. So I’m saying no. It would be costly, it would be ugly, and continuing something that should have been better handled the first time, but it could be wrapped up quite well without spending a whole lot of money, I reckon,” he added.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates.
